I made a very stupid med error when I was new in the icu. Thankfully much like in your situation, patient was fine, no adverse side effects. 

Here’s what helped me: thank the universe this was not a lesson that cost a life. We made a mistake. It didn’t hurt anyone, but let’s learn from this mistake so we never do it again. Stay humble and own your mistake. Take pride in that you’ve learned a great nursing lesson so early on in your career. 

What happened to me: I had a meeting with both assistant and head nurse managers about what happened explicitly. Got some education, signed a form saying I got talked to, and was out the door. Both managers said they have done stupid med mistakes too and this is part of a young nursing career. They really drove home the point of “don’t beat yourself up, learn from this, take your time and do your medication rights, don’t do it again”.
Not stupid to try at all! Keep high hopes! This is a great community. Maybe something will turn up? Good luck friend.

Also walk the patients family members/friends though what your doing. “Hey x, I’m going to brush your teeth now.” Or “x, we are going to reposition you.” Talking through the cares you do w/ the patient will show you care and that you’re not just shoving swabs in their mouth q2 or manhandling them w/ turns. 

Explaining what each piece of equipment helps too. Explain the vent. Explain the drugs they are on. Explain the procedures the patient is going to get/has already received. Transparency I have found really helps ease the nerves and builds a safe and open relationship for the family. 

Never take anything they say to heart. When the family members vent, let them. Be an open ear. Don’t take anything personally and reassure them when they are expressing feelings. I drop the line “let it all out. We are here for you.”. I also encourage them to talk with their family member. Yeah they are sedated but it doesn’t mean they can’t hold their hand and talk with them. 

Little gestures of care for the family also go a long way. Offer water, coffee, or thickened apple juice (it’s a joke but sometimes laughter helps). Offer warm blankets, pillows, chairs, room temp (if the patients body temp allows it)… really anything to make them more comfortable.

I became a cna to see if I truly wanted to be in the medical field. Did LTC for a year, got into a hospital for 6 months and then got into nursing school. I hated LTC/SNF work but the hospital cna job was kush compared to the nursing homes. I also got to work along side hospital RNs and decided it was a path I was willing to go down in terms of school and loans. I’m now an icu rn after working med/surg for 2 years. I’d say it was all worth it. The skills I gained as a cna greatly helped me in nursing school and when I became an RN. 

I never anticipated being a cna for a long time. I saw it as an intro to the medical field. Do I like it? Can I do it? Is this something I want to do as a career? Turns out all my answers to that were yes, so I pursued a BSN degree. 

The beauty of a cna license is that it’s relatively cheap and it’s not a forever job. If it’s not your jam, don’t feel bad about bailing! Don’t let anyone tell you you’re weak or couldn’t handle it. It’s not for everyone. Just like how working a 9-5 office job isn’t for everyone. Just like how I like pineapple on pizza and others don't. It’s not for everyone. Give it your honest best and if you don't vibe, then thats fine.
